Slide 12

One probe, hundreds of neurons

  • Neuropixels: one shank, 10 mm × 70 µm

    • Sites 20 µm apart: one neuron seen on several sites
    • Its waveform pattern across sites → spike sorting
  • One insertion: hundreds of neurons, several areas
  • Our monkey data (Bao et al. 2020): 482 neurons, one electrode at a time
    • Modern datasets: thousands per animal
Jun et al. Nature 2017 · Fig. 1 · Steinmetz et al. Science 2021 (Neuropixels 2.0: 5,120 sites)

Slide 13

Recording neural populations

a  Scales of access: scalp EEG → ECoG on the cortical surface → microelectrodes in the tissue
b  Signal chain: EEG and ECoG average many neurons; only electrodes in the tissue resolve spikes
c  ECoG grid — a flexible surface array (coin for scale)
d  Utah array — 100 silicon needles, 400 µm apart; used in human BCI
e  Silicon probe — dozens of recording sites along one shank (Neuropixels lineage)
f  Optoelectrode — micro-LEDs on the shank for optogenetics
g  Micro-ECoG — surface array fine enough for single cells
h  CMOS probe — amplifiers built into the probe base
i  Fluidic probe — electrodes plus channels for drug delivery
j  3D active array — flexible interconnect
Figure: Seymour, Wu, Wise & Yoon, Microsystems & Nanoengineering 2017 · Fig. 1 (CC BY 4.0)

Notation — table
Symbol Meaning
𝐱\mathbf{x} (bold lowercase) a vector: the whole list of numbers for one object
xjx_j (italic, subscript) its jjth component, a single number
𝐱(i)\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, 𝐱(i,r)\mathbf{x}^{(i,r)} the vector for image ii; the same image on repetition rr
𝐗\mathbf{X} (bold uppercase) a matrix: many vectors stacked, one image per row
𝐱⊤\mathbf{x}^{\top} the transpose: the same numbers laid out as a row instead of a column
∥𝐱∥\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert the length of the vector
DD, NN the number of measurements per object; the number of objects

Slide 29

A vector is an arrow from the origin

Same two numbers: a point, or an arrow from the origin to it.

𝐱(1)≈(72.740.6)(the tiger)\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\approx\begin{pmatrix}72.7\\40.6\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{(the tiger)}

  • Superscript (1)(1): image number 1
  • Arrows: what lets us add, subtract and compare

Slide 30

Extending beyond two dimensions

𝐱(i)=(x1(i)x2(i)⋮xD(i))∈ℝD\mathbf{x}^{(i)}=\begin{pmatrix}x_1^{(i)}\\x_2^{(i)}\\\vdots\\x_D^{(i)}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}

  • 𝐱(i)\mathbf{x}^{(i)}: representation of image ii, one number per measurement
  • DD: the dimension, the number of measurements
    • ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}: all such lists
  • Same object, different measurement → different DD, different space

Slide 31

Before comparing responses: how reliable is one?

A brain does not give the same answer twice.

Return to contents

Slide 32

Brain responses are noisy

  • Same image three times → three different response vectors
  • Single fMRI trial: mostly noise
  • Averaging keeps what repeats, cancels what does not
Data: Chang et al. Scientific Data 2019 · BOLD5000 CSI1, image n01641577_1229 (bullfrog), early visual region, average of two post-stimulus time points

Return to contents

Slide 33

Electrophysiology is noisy too — averaging works

  • Monkey IT, 168 sites, same image 51 times
  • Correlation rr: agreement between two patterns, 1 = identical, 0 = unrelated (defined properly below)
  • Two single trials: r=r= 0.17
  • Mean of 25 trials vs mean of the other 25: r=r= 0.69
  • Every response vector from here on is such a mean
Data: Majaj, Hong, Solomon & DiCarlo J. Neurosci. 2015, public Brain-Score assembly; responses are normalised per site, 70–170 ms window

Return to contents

Slide 34

Average repeated responses to one image

Repetition rr of RR gives 𝐱(i,r)∈ℝD\mathbf{x}^{(i,r)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. Three neurons, three repetitions (illustrative spikes/s):

𝐱(i,1)=(251),𝐱(i,2)=(432),𝐱(i,3)=(343)⟹𝐱(i)=1R∑r=1R𝐱(i,r)=(342)\mathbf{x}^{(i,1)}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{x}^{(i,2)}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{x}^{(i,3)}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\3\end{pmatrix} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{x}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{x}^{(i,r)}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\2\end{pmatrix}

  • Mean component by component: xj(i)=1R∑rxj(i,r)x_j^{(i)}=\tfrac{1}{R}\sum_r x_j^{(i,r)}
    • Neurons never averaged into one another
  • 𝐱(i)\mathbf{x}^{(i)} stands for image ii from here on; repetitions kept for reliability

Slide 35

Column vectors and row vectors

Column: DD rows, one column. Transpose ⊤^{\top}: the same numbers as a row.

𝐱(i)=(342)∈ℝ3×1→ ⊤ (𝐱(i))⊤=(342)∈ℝ1×3\mathbf{x}^{(i)}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\2\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 1} \qquad\xrightarrow{\ \top\ }\qquad \big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\big)^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}3&4&2\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 3}

  • Same numbers, same order; only the orientation changes
  • Rows: how we stack many images

Return to contents

Slide 36

Many images form a response matrix

Stack NN row vectors: one matrix for the whole image set. Two ways to write the same object:

𝐗=((𝐱(1))⊤(𝐱(2))⊤⋮(𝐱(N))⊤)=(X11X12⋯X1DX21X22⋯X2D⋮⋮⋮XN1XN2⋯XND)∈ℝN×D\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}\big(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\big)^{\top}\\\big(\mathbf{x}^{(2)}\big)^{\top}\\\vdots\\\big(\mathbf{x}^{(N)}\big)^{\top}\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}X_{11}&X_{12}&\cdots&X_{1D}\\X_{21}&X_{22}&\cdots&X_{2D}\\\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\X_{N1}&X_{N2}&\cdots&X_{ND}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}

  • Row ii: image ii. Column jj: feature jj
  • Xij=xj(i)X_{ij}=x_j^{(i)}: feature jj of image ii, one cell of the picture
  • Here: N=6N=6 images, 12 of D=4,096D=4{,}096 activations shown

Return to contents

Slide 37

One matrix to hold what a system treats as alike

Pixels, voxels, neurons, network units: different vectors, different lengths, different units. A matrix of pairwise comparisons is the one object they all share. Everything that follows builds it.

Return to contents

Slide 38

An RDM compares every pair of images

Representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM): every pairwise comparison.

𝐃∈ℝN×N,Dik=d(𝐱(i),𝐱(k))\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N},\qquad D_{ik}=d\bigl(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\bigr)

  • Rows and columns: images. Each entry: one comparison
  • dd: the comparison rule. It decides which differences count
  • Entries are not arbitrary: Dii=0D_{ii}=0, Dik=DkiD_{ik}=D_{ki}, and for a distance, no shortcut beats the direct route
Kriegeskorte & Kievit Trends in Cognitive Sciences 2013

Return to contents

Slide 40

A difference defines a direction

Subtraction: the displacement from image 1 (tiger) to image 2 (elephant):

𝐱(2)−𝐱(1)=(128.3−72.719.2−40.6)=(55.6−21.4)\mathbf{x}^{(2)}-\mathbf{x}^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}128.3-72.7\\19.2-40.6\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}55.6\\-21.4\end{pmatrix}

𝐱(2)−𝐱(1)\mathbf{x}^{(2)}-\mathbf{x}^{(1)} is itself a vector: from the tiger's point to the elephant's.

Return to contents

Slide 41

Euclidean distance

Length of the difference vector:

dEuc(𝐱(i),𝐱(k))=∥𝐱(k)−𝐱(i)∥=∑j=1D(xj(k)−xj(i))2d_{\mathrm{Euc}}\bigl(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\bigr)=\bigl\|\mathbf{x}^{(k)}-\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\bigr\|=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{D}\bigl(x_j^{(k)}-x_j^{(i)}\bigr)^2}

Tiger and elephant, 𝐱(2)−𝐱(1)=(55.6, −21.4)\mathbf{x}^{(2)}-\mathbf{x}^{(1)}=(55.6,\,-21.4):

dEuc=55.62+21.42=59.5d_{\mathrm{Euc}}=\sqrt{55.6^2+21.4^2}=59.5

Slide 43

The dot product measures alignment

Distance asks how far apart. A second question: do two vectors point the same way?

𝐰⊤𝐱=∑j=1Dwjxj=∥𝐰∥ ∥𝐱∥cos⁡ϕ\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\sum_{j=1}^{D}w_j x_j=\|\mathbf{w}\|\,\|\mathbf{x}\|\cos\phi

  • Multiply matching components, add
  • Equal to the product of the lengths times cos⁡ϕ\cos\phi, ϕ\phi the angle between them
  • 𝐰=(1,1)/2\mathbf{w}=(1,1)/\sqrt2 (length 1), tiger 𝐱(1)=(72.7, 40.6)\mathbf{x}^{(1)}=(72.7,\,40.6): 𝐰⊤𝐱(1)=80.1\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{(1)}=80.1, the length of the tiger's shadow on 𝐰\mathbf{w}

Return to contents

Slide 44

Two similarity measures: cosine and correlation

scos⁡(𝐱(i),𝐱(k))=cos⁡ϕ=𝐱(i)⊤𝐱(k)∥𝐱(i)∥ ∥𝐱(k)∥r(𝐱(i),𝐱(k))=𝐱c(i)⊤𝐱c(k)∥𝐱c(i)∥ ∥𝐱c(k)∥,𝐱c=𝐱−xˉ 𝟏s_{\cos}\bigl(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\bigr)=\cos\phi=\frac{\mathbf{x}^{(i)\top}\mathbf{x}^{(k)}}{\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\|\,\|\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\|}\qquad\qquad r\bigl(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\bigr)=\frac{\mathbf{x}_c^{(i)\top}\mathbf{x}_c^{(k)}}{\|\mathbf{x}_c^{(i)}\|\,\|\mathbf{x}_c^{(k)}\|},\quad \mathbf{x}_c=\mathbf{x}-\bar{x}\,\mathbf{1}

  • Cosine similarity: the dot product with both lengths divided out. 1 = same direction, 0 = perpendicular
  • Correlation (Pearson rr): cosine similarity after subtracting each pattern's own mean xˉ\bar{x}
  • Both are similarities: large when alike. A dissimilarity is the flip: dcos⁡=1−scos⁡d_{\cos}=1-s_{\cos}, dcorr=1−rd_{\mathrm{corr}}=1-r
SciPy · spatial.distance

Slide 47

One thing to know about artificial neurons before comparing their responses

Network activations are not firing rates. Many of them are exactly zero, by design. That changes what a comparison rule sees.

Return to contents

Slide 48

Why network responses contain zeros

ReLU (rectified linear unit): input zjz_j, output aj=max⁡(0,zj)a_j=\max(0,z_j).

Nonlinearity: stacked layers become more than one linear map.

Torchvision · ResNet · PyTorch · ReLU

Return to contents

Shared zeros can change correlation

Drop the 879 shared zeros: correlation dissimilarity 0.897 → 1.011.

Euclidean and cosine: unchanged.

Slide 50

Two unit steps cannot span three units

Can an RDM hold any numbers? Try D12=1D_{12}=1, D23=1D_{23}=1, D13=3D_{13}=3.

Euclidean requires D13≤D12+D23=2D_{13}\leq D_{12}+D_{23}=2.

Slide 51

Which comparisons are metrics?

A rule dd is a metric when Dik=d(𝐱(i),𝐱(k))D_{ik}=d(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{x}^{(k)}) meets four requirements for every triple of images:

Which comparisons are metrics? — table
Requirement Mathematical statement Euclidean dEucd_{\mathrm{Euc}} Cosine dcos⁡d_{\cos} Correlation dcorrd_{\mathrm{corr}}
Nonnegativity Dik≥0D_{ik}\ge0 ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ Yes
Identity Dik=0  ⟺  𝐱(i)=𝐱(k)D_{ik}=0\iff\mathbf{x}^{(i)}=\mathbf{x}^{(k)} ✓ Yes ✗ No ✗ No
Symmetry Dik=DkiD_{ik}=D_{ki} ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ Yes
Triangle inequality Dil≤Dik+DklD_{il}\le D_{ik}+D_{kl} ✓ Yes ✗ No ✗ No
Metric on these vectors? All four requirements ✓ Yes ✗ No ✗ No

Cosine requires nonzero vectors; correlation requires nonconstant vectors.
✓ holds throughout the domain; ✗ can fail, even when the measure is defined.

Return to contents

Slide 52

Cosine dissimilarity is not a metric

For cosine dissimilarity, Dik=dcos⁡(𝐱(i),𝐱(k))D_{ik}=d_{\cos}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\mathbf{x}^{(k)}).

D13=1,D_{13}=1,

D12+D23=2−2≈0.586.D_{12}+D_{23}=2-\sqrt2\approx0.586.

Triangle inequality: violated.

Identity too: (1,0)(1,0) and (2,0)(2,0) have zero cosine dissimilarity.

A1 §1b–d: simple vectors first, then real images and activations.

Slide 53

Training changes the representation

  • The RDMs above came from a trained network. Where did that structure come from?
  • Weights: the adjustable numbers inside the network. Training: find weights that reduce the classification loss on labeled images

Return to contents

Slide 54

What training does to the RDM

  • Same six images, same architecture, two sets of weights
  • Random weights: every pair looks alike (1−r≈0.151-r\approx0.15). The network barely tells the images apart
  • Trained: every pair far apart (1−r≈0.951-r\approx0.95). Training pulled the six animals apart
  • The RDM is not a property of the architecture. It is a property of the weights
Correlation distance on the 4,096 stored late-layer activations · random weights, seed 1291 · figures/make_L01_rdm_trained_untrained.py

Return to contents

Slide 55

With many images: training pulls categories together

  • Same 1,224 images, same architecture, two sets of weights†
  • Trained: same-category images move together. Random weights: categories stay mixed
  • How weights get there: backpropagation, a few lectures away. Preview: 3Blue1Brown, But what is a neural network?
† 512 numbers per image reduced to two for plotting (PCA, covered later) · random weights, seed 1291 · Bao et al. Nature 2020 images

Return to contents

Slide 56

Representations and comparisons

  • A measurement: one vector per object
  • Components: coordinates. Many objects: a response matrix
  • Difference: a direction. Its length: Euclidean distance. Dot product: alignment
  • Similarity (cosine, correlation) and dissimilarity (its flip) are choices; each ignores something different. Not every rule is a metric
  • RDM: every pairwise comparison in one matrix. Next lecture: RDM → map
  • A network's RDM comes from its weights, and the weights from training

Return to contents

Want to see inside a network before we get there?

Two lectures on convolutional networks and one on training are coming. Previews:

  • 3Blue1Brown — But what is a neural network? (19 min). Pixels → activations, layer by layer, on digits. The best single video.
  • Harley — draw a digit, watch a network read it. Live activations; hover a unit for its inputs. The convolutional version is there too.
  • CNN Explainer (Georgia Tech). Convolution, ReLU and pooling on the actual numbers; upload your own image.
  • Yosinski — Deep Visualization Toolbox (4 min). A webcam through AlexNet, every layer on screen.
  • TensorFlow Playground. Tiny networks on 2-D toy data; watch the decision surface train. Closest to the next lectures.

Not required. Ten minutes well spent: the explainer and the playground.

Slide 58

Further reading for the research trail

Six starting points, none required. Pick one, skim it, and post on Ed. Peterson et al. 2018 and Bao et al. 2020 are the assignment papers: fine to read, but branch out.

  • DiCarlo, Zoccolan & Rust 2012, Neuron — how the brain solves object recognition: the pathway on our recording slides, and the case for population codes
  • Kriegeskorte, Mur & Bandettini 2008, Front. Syst. Neurosci. — the RDM as a common currency across recordings, imaging, behaviour and models
  • Kriegeskorte & Kievit 2013, Trends Cogn. Sci. — representational geometry, the survey
  • Yamins & DiCarlo 2016, Nat. Neurosci. — why networks trained on a task predict neural responses
  • Geirhos et al. 2019, ICLR — texture bias: what a network's similarity structure keys on
  • Bowers et al. 2023, Behav. Brain Sci. — the critique: when a good prediction score is not evidence

Return to contents

Slide 59

How to read for the trail

  • Skim first: abstract, figures, last paragraph of the discussion. Then decide whether to read
  • Ask what would change the conclusion
    • Is a control missing?
    • Would another network, another animal, another image set give the same result?
    • Is the result trivial given the method?
  • Expect it to be slow at first. It gets faster; the questions become habits
  • Then post: four to six sentences on Ed, one reply to a classmate

Write three brief points in your own words:

  1. One sentence: when can two response vectors have zero cosine dissimilarity but a large Euclidean distance?
  2. Something you do not yet understand, or a question still open
  3. Another idea you found interesting, and why it matters for brains, behavior or AI

Credit for a thoughtful attempt, not for being correct.

Reference: computing an RDM

import numpy as np from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist, squareform X = np.array([[1., 1.], # pattern A [4., 4.], # pattern B [1., -1.]]) # pattern C for metric in ("euclidean", "cosine"): D = squareform(pdist(X, metric=metric)) print(metric, np.round(D, 2))

pdist: the unique pairs. squareform: the symmetric matrix.
